ortho.salvation:
Orthodox Christians speak of salvation as the healing and restoration of the human person in communion with the Holy Trinity. It is not only a verdict declared over us, but a lifelong sharing in the life of Christ, begun in Baptism and Chrismation, nourished in the Holy Mysteries, and completed in the resurrection of the body.

This path is often named theosis: by grace we become partakers of the divine nature, without ever becoming what God is by essence. Salvation is synergy. God acts first and always; we respond with repentance, faith, and a life of love. The Church does not treat salvation as a single private moment that cannot be lost, nor as a human achievement. It is Christ's victory received in the Church.
ortho.trinity:
The Holy Trinity is the living God whom the Church confesses: one God in three consubstantial Persons, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. The Father is the source, the Son is begotten of the Father before all ages, and the Spirit proceeds from the Father. There is one essence, one will, and one energy, yet three hypostases who are not roles or masks.

Orthodox worship is Trinitarian from first doxology to last. We do not begin from an abstract One and then add Persons. We know the Father through the Son in the Holy Spirit. Any account that divides the Three into three gods, or collapses them into one person, is foreign to the Church's faith.
ortho.father:
God the Father is the unoriginate source of the Godhead. He is not first among equals in a committee of gods, nor a lonely monad who later becomes three. From him the Son is begotten and the Spirit proceeds. All things exist from the Father, through the Son, in the Holy Spirit.

When Orthodox pray 'Our Father,' they address this Person, not a generic deity. The Father is known only through the Son, who said that whoever has seen him has seen the Father. The monarchy of the Father safeguards both the unity of God and the real distinction of the Persons.
ortho.holy_spirit:
The Holy Spirit is the third Person of the Holy Trinity, Lord and Giver of life, who proceeds from the Father and rests in the Son. He is not a force or mood of God, but the Spirit who spoke by the prophets, descended at Pentecost, and is given in Chrismation.

In the Church the Spirit makes Christ present, constitutes the Eucharist, imparts the charismata, and leads the faithful into all truth. Orthodox piety asks the Spirit to come and abide in us. The Spirit does not replace Christ or invent a new gospel; he glorifies the Son and brings us to the Father.
ortho.filioque:
The Church confesses that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father. That is the language of the Creed as received in the East and of the Lord's own words. Procession from the Father names the Spirit's eternal origin. The Spirit is sent in time through the Son, and rests upon the Son, but eternal procession is from the Father alone.

Orthodox concern about the Filioque is not a quarrel over a syllable. Adding 'and the Son' to the Creed, without an ecumenical council of the whole Church, appeared to confuse the Father's unique monarchy and to treat the Spirit as junior. Dialogue continues, yet the received Orthodox confession remains procession from the Father.
ortho.essence_and_energies:
Orthodox theology distinguishes God's essence from his energies. The essence is God as he is in himself, utterly beyond creaturely grasp. The energies are God himself as he truly gives himself: grace, glory, the uncreated light seen by the saints. We do not know God by climbing into his essence; we know him by participation in his energies.

This is why theosis is possible. God remains God, and we remain creatures, yet we are really united to him. Grace is not a created thing inserted between God and the soul. It is the living God acting. The distinction is not two gods, but a way of speaking faithfully about communion without confusion.
ortho.incarnation:
The Incarnation is the Son of God taking flesh from the Theotokos and becoming man without ceasing to be God. The Word became flesh and dwelt among us. There is one Lord Jesus Christ, perfect in divinity and perfect in humanity, whose coming is the healing of our nature.

Orthodox faith will not separate the man Jesus from the eternal Son, nor dissolve the humanity into a mere appearance. What is not assumed is not healed. Therefore he took a complete human nature, body and rational soul, from the Virgin, and in that nature he lived, died, rose, and remains forever.
ortho.natures_of_christ:
Following the Council of Chalcedon as the Church received it, Orthodox confess two natures in the one hypostasis of the Word: fully God and fully man, without change, without confusion, without division, without separation. The hypostatic union means the Person is one; the natures remain what they are.

We refuse both a Christ who is only a God wearing flesh and a Christ who is a man later adopted by God. The same One worked miracles and suffered hunger. The communication of properties belongs to the one Person. Later Orthodox writers also honor the intent of the non-Chalcedonian churches while remaining within Chalcedonian language.
ortho.virgin_birth:
The Church confesses the virgin birth: Christ was conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary. His humanity is taken from her; his Person is the eternal Son. The birth does not violate her virginity. It is a new creation, not the ordinary fruit of human seed.

This is not a decorative miracle. It proclaims that salvation comes from God, and that the new Adam enters the race without the broken inheritance of the old. Icons of the Nativity and the hymns of the feast keep this confession before the people year after year.
ortho.preexistence_of_christ:
The Son is not a creature who began. He is begotten of the Father before all ages: eternal generation, not an event in time. There was never a when when the Son was not. The Word who became flesh is the One through whom all things were made.

Orthodox preaching therefore will not speak of Jesus as a man who later became divine, nor as the first of God's works. Preexistence here means true God from true God. The Child in the manger is the Ancient of Days, as the Nativity hymn sings.
ortho.atonement:
The atonement is Christ's whole work of assuming our nature, living in obedience, dying on the Cross, descending to Hades, and rising. Orthodox preaching uses many images: victory over death and the devil, ransom, healing, sacrifice, illumination. No single Latin theory is made the only key.

He dies for us and with us, trampling down death by death. The Cross is not the Father punishing a third party to satisfy an honor code. It is the love of the Trinity overthrowing corruption and setting captives free. We enter that victory by dying and rising with him in Baptism and by a life of repentance.
ortho.resurrection_of_christ:
The Resurrection is the heart of Orthodox faith and the feast of feasts, Pascha. Christ is risen from the dead, trampling down death by death. His risen body is the same body that suffered, now glorified, the firstfruits of those who sleep.

Without the Resurrection our preaching is empty. Icons, the midnight Gospel, and the forty days of Pascha teach that death is not the last word. The Resurrection is not a metaphor for spring or for the disciples' feelings. It is the bodily rising of the incarnate Word, in which our own rising is already begun.
ortho.ascension:
Forty days after Pascha the Church keeps the Ascension. The risen Lord is taken up and sits at the right hand of the Father, still bearing our humanity. He does not shed the flesh he assumed. Our nature is carried into the heavens.

The Ascension is not an absence. He promised to be with us always, and he sends the Spirit. From the Father's right hand he intercedes and will come again. The icon shows the disciples and the Theotokos beneath the departing Christ, already turned toward the Church's life in history.
ortho.gifts_of_the_spirit:
The charismata are gifts of the Holy Spirit for the building up of the Church: wisdom, healing, discernment, prophecy, tongues in the apostolic sense, and the quieter gifts of governance, hospitality, and teaching. They are given as the Spirit wills, ordinarily within the sacramental and ascetic life of the Church.

Orthodox Christianity does not treat extraordinary signs as the normal proof of the Spirit, nor does it declare that the Spirit has withdrawn his gifts. Saints throughout the ages have healed and discerned. The surest gifts are repentance, humility, and love. Any charism that divides the Church or bypasses her bishops is received with caution.
ortho.justification:
Justification in Orthodox speech is being made righteous by communion with Christ, not a bare legal fiction. When the publican went down to his house justified, he was set right with God. Baptism washes, Chrismation seals, and the life of repentance continues that healing.

We do not usually split justification and sanctification into two separate events. Both name the one work of grace. Faith is living and active. We are justified by grace through faith that works by love, in the Church, not by collecting merits or by a once-for-all declaration that leaves the heart unchanged.
ortho.sanctification:
Sanctification is the Spirit's work of making us holy, which is the ordinary word for the Christian life after Baptism. It is growth in the likeness of God, the cleansing of the passions, and the acquisition of the virtues. The Holy Mysteries, prayer, fasting, almsgiving, and obedience to a spiritual father are its school.

It is never finished in this age. Even the saints call themselves sinners. Sanctification is not moral self-improvement beside grace. It is the same grace that justifies, now stretching through a lifetime until the resurrection.
ortho.theosis:
Theosis is the goal of the Christian life: union with God by grace, becoming partakers of the divine nature. We do not become the Holy Trinity by essence. We become by energy what God is, as iron in the fire becomes fire yet remains iron.

This is the meaning of salvation in its fullness. Baptism plants it, the Eucharist feeds it, prayer and ascesis uncover it. Athanasius said the Word became man that we might become god, meaning deified creatures. The uncreated light of Tabor is the same glory offered to the saints.
ortho.grace:
Grace is God himself acting, often called uncreated grace or the divine energies. It is not a thing God hands over and then leaves. Every good in us is grace, and our free response is itself enabled by grace. The Church's Mysteries are wellsprings of this life.

Created 'helps' may prepare us, but they are not a substitute for communion with the living God. Cheap grace that asks no repentance is not Orthodox teaching, nor is a grace so scarce that human effort must earn God's favor.
ortho.faith_and_works:
Faith and works are not rivals. Living faith is trust in Christ that immediately takes the shape of repentance, mercy, and keeping the commandments. Synergy means God initiates and we cooperate; without him we can do nothing, yet he does not save us as stones.

James is read with Paul. Works without faith are empty, and faith without works is dead. Orthodox ethics is not a ladder of merits. It is the fruit of the Spirit in a healed heart. The thief on the cross shows that grace can gather a whole life into one hour of faith.
ortho.predestination:
God foreknows all things and wills that all be saved. Orthodox teaching is wary of a decree that some are created for damnation apart from their response. Predestination is spoken of in the Fathers as God's purpose in Christ, not as a hidden list that cancels freedom.

We confess foreknowledge and providence without making human persons puppets. The mystery remains. Pastoral preaching calls everyone to repentance, because no one is entitled to despair of mercy or to presume upon it.
ortho.assurance:
Assurance in Orthodox life is hope, not a private certificate that one cannot fall. We know whom we have believed, and we work out our salvation with fear and trembling. Frequent confession, communion, and the prayers of the Church give a sober confidence.

Presumption and despair are both passions. The saints combine boldness toward God with the cry 'Lord, have mercy.' A Christian may be confident in Christ's faithfulness without claiming to see the end of his own story before the judgment.
ortho.repentance:
Repentance, metanoia, is a change of mind and a turning of the whole life toward God. It is not a single tearful episode but the air the Orthodox Christian breathes. Confession before the priest, tears, restitution, and a new way of walking are its signs.

The Church's year is shaped by seasons of repentance, above all Great Lent. No sin is beyond forgiveness except the despair that refuses to ask. Repentance is joy, not self-hatred: the Father runs to meet the prodigal.
ortho.original_sin:
Orthodox commonly speak of ancestral sin rather than inherited guilt. In Adam death and corruption entered the race. We are born into a wounded world and a wounded nature, inclined to the passions, and we need healing from our first breath. We do not inherit Adam's personal culpability as if we committed his act.

Baptism of infants is therefore not the cancellation of a baby’s courtroom guilt but entrance into the life that overcomes death. Personal sins are our own. The Fall is real; its healing is Christ.
ortho.human_nature:
Human nature was created good, in the image of God, and remains essentially good even after the Fall. It is darkened and mortal, not turned into evil substance. The Incarnation assumes this nature in order to restore it.

Ascesis fights the passions that parasitically use nature, not nature itself. Body and soul together are the person. Orthodox anthropology refuses both contempt for the body and the idea that we are free of deep damage.
ortho.image_of_god:
The image and likeness of God name our capacity for communion with him: reason, freedom, relationality, and the call to grow into likeness. The image is not erased by the Fall; the likeness is darkened and must be restored in Christ.

Every human being, without exception, bears the image and is therefore inviolable. Theosis is the likeness brought to fullness. Icons of Christ and the saints are possible because the image has been renewed in the Incarnation.
ortho.free_will:
Free will remains after the Fall, though weakened and in need of grace. Synergy is the Orthodox word: we cannot save ourselves, and God will not save us without us. The commandments assume that we can respond.

This is not Pelagian self-rescue. Grace goes before, accompanies, and completes every good act. It is also not a bondage so total that responsibility disappears. The Fathers warn against both pride in our choosing and fatalism.
ortho.mortal_and_venial_sin:
Orthodox speech about sin is less a two-tier legal code than a physician's account of the passions. Some sins slay the life of grace in us; others wound it. There is no official list matching the Latin mortal and venial scheme, though grave sins are known and named in confession.

What matters is turning back. A hard heart can make a small act deadly; a repentant heart can bring a great fall to healing. The priest as physician helps discern the difference.
ortho.total_depravity:
Orthodox teaching affirms a deep corruption of nature after the Fall, but not total depravity in the sense that nothing good remains and the will cannot respond at all. The image of God is obscured, not annihilated. Catechumens can seek Baptism; the prodigal can come to himself.

We need grace for every step. We do not need to be told that we are so ruined that cooperation is impossible. Corruption is real enough that only the death and resurrection of Christ can heal it.
ortho.scripture:
Holy Scripture is the Church's book, God-breathed and given for salvation. The Gospel is proclaimed from it in every Liturgy. We kiss the Gospel book because Christ speaks there.

Scripture is not an orphan text waiting for each reader to found a church upon it. It is heard inside Holy Tradition, with the Fathers, the councils, and the liturgical life. Private novelty that contradicts the mind of the Church is not the Spirit's work.
ortho.canon:
The canon of Scripture is the list the Church reads as the word of God. The New Testament books are those of the whole Church. The Old Testament in Orthodox use includes books often called deuterocanonical or anagignoskomena, read in the services, though local listing of the exact edges has known some variation.

The Church did not receive a table of contents from heaven apart from her life. She recognized the books that had fed her from the beginning. No later private list overrules that reception.
ortho.sola_scriptura:
Orthodox Christians receive Scripture and Holy Tradition as one stream of the Spirit's life in the Church, not as two rival sources and not as Scripture standing alone over against the Church. The Bible is supreme among written witnesses, yet it is never stripped from the worship, canons, and Fathers that handed it on.

Sola scriptura as a principle that each believer or each era may restart Christianity from the text alone is not our rule. The same Spirit who inspired the writers abides in the Church.
ortho.inspiration:
Inspiration means the Spirit spoke through the prophets and apostles so that Scripture is truly God's word in human words. It is not dictation that erases the writer's voice, nor a merely human book later stamped holy.

Because it is inspired, it is trustworthy for the knowledge of God and the way of salvation. The Church reads it christologically. Christ is the key; isolated verses used against the Church's faith are misread.
ortho.inerrancy:
Orthodox speak of the truth of Scripture: it does not deceive us in what God intends to teach for our salvation. The Fathers can note difficulties of text and history without treating the Bible as a trap.

Modern inerrancy debates framed in forensic English are not native to us. We do not need to claim that every chronological detail satisfies a modern historian in order to confess that the Scriptures are true and holy. Their truth is proved in the Church's life and in the saints they form.
ortho.apocrypha:
Books sometimes called deuterocanonical are read in Orthodox worship and theology: Wisdom, Sirach, Tobit, Maccabees, Baruch, and others according to local usage. They are Scripture in the Church's practice even where some writers ranked them with a nuance different from the Law and the Gospel.

We do not call them a Protestant 'Apocrypha' to be kept off the lectern. They feed the feasts, the prayers for the departed, and the moral teaching of the Fathers.
ortho.hermeneutics:
Interpretation in the Church means Scripture is read with Christ at the center, in the liturgy, and with the Fathers. The mind of the Church, not the isolated modern self, is the interpreter. Typology, the rule of faith, and the living experience of holiness guide the reading.

Scholarship is welcome as a servant. It does not sit in judgment on the Creed. Where the saints agree, we are slow to invent a new sense. Where they differ on a passage, we do not pretend a later theory has closed the matter.
ortho.tradition:
Holy Tradition is the life of the Holy Spirit in the Church: Scripture, the Creed, the councils, the Liturgy, the canons, the Fathers, the icons, and the lives of the saints. It is not a museum of customs and not a license for every local habit.

Tradition hands on the same Gospel. It can distinguish apostolic tradition from mere custom. To stand in Tradition is to stand in the communion of the undivided Church, not to freeze the fourth century as a costume.
ortho.magisterium:
Orthodox do not locate teaching authority in a single office over the whole Church. The mind of the Church is expressed in the consensus of the Fathers, the ecumenical councils, the episcopate in council, and the faithful who receive the faith. A bishop teaches; he does not replace the Church.

Reception matters. A council is ecumenical when the Church recognizes in it the apostolic faith. Private theological opinions, even of great men, remain opinions until the Church lives them.
ortho.papal_primacy:
Orthodox have long granted the Bishop of Rome a primacy of honor among the ancient patriarchates, as first among equals in the taxis of the first millennium. That honor is not universal immediate jurisdiction over every diocese, nor infallible power to define dogma by himself.

The rupture with Rome is read in the East as a claim that exceeded conciliar communion. Any restored primacy, in Orthodox hope, would look like the first-millennium model of presidency in love, not a substitute for the synod of bishops.
ortho.papal_infallibility:
The infallibility of the Church belongs to the Church as a whole when she speaks the apostolic faith, especially in an ecumenical council received by the people of God. It is not located in one bishop speaking ex cathedra apart from the Church.

Orthodox therefore cannot accept papal infallibility as defined in the Latin West. This is not a denial that the Spirit guides the Church. It is a different map of where that guidance is recognized.
ortho.ecumenical_councils:
The Orthodox Church receives seven ecumenical councils, from Nicaea to Nicaea II, as the dogmatic backbone of the faith: Trinity, Christology, and the holy icons. Later local councils of great weight, such as those that confirmed Palamite teaching, are honored without always receiving the title 'eighth ecumenical.'

A council is not true merely because emperors summoned it. It is true when it bears witness to what the Church has always believed. The seven are the common Orthodox list.
ortho.apostolic_succession:
Apostolic succession is the handing on of the episcopal office by prayer and the laying on of hands in the one Church, together with succession in the apostolic faith. Hands without the faith, or faith without the Church's ministry, do not suffice by themselves in Orthodox understanding.

Bishops stand in the place of the apostles as shepherds, not as a twelfth-century corporation. Through them the Eucharist is the same sacrifice and banquet. Succession is a living chain, not a museum certificate.
ortho.priesthood_authority:
The priesthood is Christ's priesthood shared with the Church. Bishops and presbyters serve it in a particular way; the royal priesthood of the baptized is real and is not a slogan against Holy Orders. Authority is for feeding the flock, celebrating the Mysteries, and guarding the faith.

It is not personal ownership of grace. A priest who falls can be deposed. The people of God surround the altar. Clericalism that treats the parish as a private chapel contradicts the rite itself.
ortho.church:
The Church is the Body of Christ, the temple of the Spirit, the communion of the Holy Trinity opened to the world. She is one, holy, catholic, and apostolic. She is not a voluntary society of the like-minded, nor only an invisible roster known to God.

To be in the Church is to be in eucharistic communion with her bishops and her people. The Church includes the saints and the faithful departed. She is both gift and task: already the Kingdom in mystery, still on pilgrimage.
ortho.one_true_church:
Orthodox confess that the Orthodox Church is the one, holy, catholic, and apostolic Church. This is a statement about identity, not a claim that God's mercy is imprisoned or that every non-Orthodox person is damned.

How the Church names those outside her canonical bounds varies among theologians: some speak more strictly, some more generously about vestiges of the Church. Official speech usually avoids both cheap indifference and cheap condemnation. The call is to the fullness of the faith in Orthodox communion.
ortho.great_apostasy:
The Church did not fail. Christ promised that the gates of Hades would not prevail. Orthodox history knows heresy, corruption, and political captivity, yet the faith of the apostles continues in the same Body, with the same Mysteries.

A theory that the whole Church vanished for centuries and had to be refounded is incompatible with this promise. Reform and repentance are constant. Replacement of the Church is not.
ortho.marks_of_the_church:
The four marks of the Creed describe the Church: one, holy, catholic, and apostolic. Oneness is eucharistic and dogmatic communion. Holiness is Christ's holiness shared with sinners in the making. Catholicity is fullness of faith in each local church. Apostolicity is faith and succession from the apostles.

These marks are not advertising slogans. They judge us when we live below them. A community that lacks them is not made the Church by sincerity alone.
ortho.visible_and_invisible_church:
The Church is visible. She has bishops, altars, baptized people, and public worship. There is no Orthodox habit of splitting an invisible true church from a visible mixed organization as if the real Church were only a list in heaven.

God alone knows the spiritual state of each heart, and not every canonical member is a saint. That mystery does not make the Church invisible. Communion is concrete: one cup, one bishop, one faith.
ortho.polity:
Conciliarity, or synodality, is the Orthodox form of church government. Each local church is headed by a bishop; bishops meet in synod; autocephalous churches order their own life in communion with the others. There is no single bishop ruling the entire Church by ordinary jurisdiction.

Primates preside; they do not replace the synod. Parish priests serve with the bishop's blessing. This polity is theological, not merely administrative: the Trinity is communion, and so is the Church.
ortho.ecumenism:
Ecumenism names contact and conversation with other Christians. Orthodox participation has ranged from warm witness to deep suspicion. Some see it as commanded charity and a duty to speak the truth; others see it as a danger of indifferentism.

The Church has no single political program for these meetings. What is not in dispute is that unity cannot be manufactured by papering over dogma. True unity would be unity in the apostolic faith and the Eucharist.
ortho.schism:
Schism is the tearing of eucharistic communion. It is a wound in the Body, distinct from heresy though they often travel together. To break from one's bishop without just cause, or to set altar against altar, is schism.

Healing schism requires repentance and a return to communion, not a new brand. The great divisions of Christian history remain a grief. Orthodox treat them as real ruptures, not as equal branches of one tree by default.
ortho.ordination:
Ordination, cheirotonia, is the bishop's laying on of hands with the prayer of the Church, making a man deacon, presbyter, or bishop. It is a Holy Mystery, not a hiring ceremony. The candidate is called from among the people; the people cry Axios.

Grace for ministry is given, and the man remains accountable. Simony and ambition are sins against the Mystery. There is no self-made priest in Orthodoxy.
ortho.priesthood:
The priesthood of the parish is the presbyter's share in the bishop's priesthood, which is Christ's. He stands at the altar, blesses, teaches, and absolves with the bishop's authority. The baptized share the royal priesthood of offering themselves, but they do not preside at the Eucharist.

Priesthood is fatherhood, not a career ladder. In the Divine Liturgy the priest is both the one who offers and the one who is offered, in Christ.
ortho.episcopacy:
The bishop, episkopos, is the successor of the apostles in a local church, high priest of the Eucharist, teacher of the faith, and shepherd. Without a bishop there is no complete local church. He is not a regional manager; he is the living center of communion.

Bishops are chosen from among celibate clergy, ordinarily monastics. They serve in synod. A bishop who abandons the faith abandons his throne in the Church's eyes, even if civil power still names him.
ortho.deacons:
The deacon serves the Liturgy, the poor, and the bishop. He does not celebrate the Eucharist. His stole and litanies are the Church's voice of intercession. In many places the diaconate is a full and permanent ministry, not only a stepping stone.

Deaconesses existed in the early Church for ministry among women; whether and how that order should be restored is discussed, not settled as a worldwide practice.
ortho.papacy:
The Pope of Rome is, for Orthodox, the bishop of an ancient and honored see who is not at present in communion with the Orthodox Church. We remember a first-millennium presidency among patriarchs. We do not receive the later Latin claims as the constitution of the Church.

Respect for the Roman church's martyrs and Fathers remains. Communion, when it is sought, would have to be communion in faith, not absorption under a supreme pontiff as now defined in the West.
ortho.clerical_celibacy:
Married parish clergy are the norm in Orthodoxy: a man may marry before ordination to the diaconate or priesthood and remain with his wife. Bishops are taken from the celibate, almost always monastic, clergy. Second marriage after ordination is not permitted.

Celibacy is a high gift, not a requirement for every priest. The priest's family is part of parish life. This discipline is ancient in the East and is not treated as a defect waiting to be westernized.
ortho.baptism:
Baptism is the Mystery of new birth in water and the Spirit, union with Christ's death and resurrection, forgiveness of sins, and entrance into the Church. It is ordinarily triple immersion in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, immediately followed by Chrismation and communion, even for infants.

Baptism is not a later badge of a decision already complete. It is the decision's beginning in the Church's womb. Emergency baptism can be supplied; reception of some already baptized in other communities varies by economy.
ortho.infant_baptism:
Infant baptism is the Church's ordinary practice. Children of the faithful are baptized, chrismated, and communed so that they grow up inside the life of grace, not outside it waiting for an age of reason. Faith is the Church's faith in which the child is held.

Sponsors answer for the child. Personal appropriation comes with years, confession, and discipleship. To delay Baptism as if grace were unsafe for babies is foreign to Orthodox instinct.
ortho.mode_of_baptism:
Triple immersion is the Orthodox rule, imaging the three days in the tomb and the threefold Name. Pouring is used in necessity. A little water sprinkled as a mere ceremony is not the Church's mind for a normal Baptism.

The mode preaches the doctrine. We go down into death and come up in newness of life. Converts from other communities may be baptized, chrismated, or received by confession according to the bishop's economy and the previous rite.
ortho.confirmation:
Chrismation is the seal of the gift of the Holy Spirit, given with holy chrism blessed by the bishop, usually at the same service as Baptism. It is not a teenage graduation from church school. The newly baptized, including infants, are chrismated and then receive the Eucharist.

In this Mystery Pentecost becomes personal. Converts already baptized in some other communities are often received by Chrismation. The Spirit is not an optional second stage for the enthusiastic.
ortho.confession:
Confession, the Mystery of Repentance, is the healing of baptismal grace when it has been wounded by sin. The penitent speaks before the priest, who stands as witness; God forgives. The prayer of absolution is a real loosing.

It is medicine, not a turnstile. A spiritual father may give a rule of prayer or a period of abstinence from communion as therapy, not as a price paid to God. Regular confession is expected of those who commune.
ortho.anointing_of_the_sick:
Holy Unction is the Mystery of oil for the sick, for healing of soul and body and for the forgiveness of sins. It is not reserved only for the dying. In many churches it is served for the whole parish in Holy Week as well as at sickbeds.

Healing may be recovery, or the strength to die in peace, or both. The oil does not replace physicians. It places illness inside the Cross and Resurrection.
ortho.holy_orders:
Holy Orders are the Mysteries that make deacons, priests, and bishops. The three degrees are apostolic. Ordination is performed by a bishop with the prayer of the clergy and people. Women are not ordained to these three degrees in Orthodox practice.

Orders exist for the Eucharist and the care of souls. They are not a caste. Deposition is possible. The dignity of the office never excuses the man from the commandments.
ortho.matrimony:
The Mystery of Marriage, the crowning, joins a man and a woman in a union blessed as an image of Christ and the Church. The priest crowns them; the Church is the minister of the blessing, not only a witness to a private contract.

Marriage is ordered to faithful love and, when God grants, to children. It is dissolved only with sorrow, under economia, after grave failure. A second crowning may be permitted with a penitential rite. Same-sex unions are not this Mystery.
ortho.sacraments:
The Holy Mysteries are the Church's actions in which the Holy Spirit makes Christ's saving work present. Baptism, Chrismation, the Eucharist, Confession, Unction, Orders, and Marriage are commonly numbered, yet Orthodox are not anxious to lock the count at seven as if grace ran only through a list.

Monastic tonsure, the funeral, and the blessing of water are also holy. The Mysteries are neither bare symbols nor magic. They require the Church, the prayer, and the disposition of a living heart.
ortho.real_presence:
In the Eucharist there is the Real Presence of the Body and Blood of Christ. After the epiclesis we do not speak of remaining common bread and wine. The change of the gifts is confessed without requiring a scholastic account of substance and accidents.

We receive the risen Lord, not a memory only and not a new incarnation. Preparation, fasting, and confession guard the mystery. The gifts are treated as holy before, during, and after the Liturgy.
ortho.eucharistic_sacrifice:
The Divine Liturgy is the bloodless sacrifice: the one sacrifice of Christ made present, the Church's offering of praise, and the banquet of the Kingdom. We do not crucify him again. We are taken to the one offering.

Calvary and the empty tomb, not a new victim, stand on the altar. The priest and people offer and are offered. This language is sacrificial because Scripture and the Liturgy are sacrificial.
ortho.closed_communion:
Closed communion means the Eucharist is for those baptized, chrismated, and in communion with the Orthodox Church, living in repentance. It is not a sign of hospitality at a shared table of many faiths. It is the meal of one Body.

Visitors are welcomed at the Liturgy and may receive antidoron. Communion itself says something that politeness cannot unsay. Economy belongs to the bishop, not to private warmth.
ortho.liturgy:
The Divine Liturgy is the Church's central act, the Eucharist of St John Chrysostom or St Basil, with other rites in various local churches. Heaven and earth meet. It is not a program of religious entertainment surrounding a sermon.

Standing, chanting, incense, icons, and the movement from Word to Anaphora form a single prayer. The people are not an audience. 'Liturgy' means the people's work. Private devotion finds its home inside this common offering.
ortho.prayer:
Prayer is communion with God: liturgical, personal, and unceasing. The hours, the Psalms, the Jesus Prayer, and spontaneous cries for mercy belong together. Noetic prayer, the prayer of the heart, is the inner fruit the monks seek and the parish is not forbidden.

Prayer is Trinitarian and ecclesial even when said alone. We pray in the Spirit, to the Father, through the Son, with the saints. Dryness is not failure. Attention is the struggle.
ortho.liturgical_calendar:
The liturgical year is the Gospel spread across time: Pascha at the center, the twelve great feasts, fasts, and the daily commemorations of saints. Time itself is baptized. Feasts of the Lord and of the Theotokos teach dogma by keeping it.

Calendars differ in places between older and revised reckonings; the disagreement is painful and practical, not a second creed. To live the year is to be catechized without a classroom.
ortho.sunday_worship:
The Lord's Day is the first day, the day of Resurrection, the little Pascha of each week. The faithful gather for the Divine Liturgy. Work yields, as far as life allows, to the Kingdom.

Saturday remains the blessed Sabbath of rest and of prayers for the dead in some usages, but the Church's Eucharistic summit is Sunday. Neglect of the Lord's Day is neglect of the rising of Christ.
ortho.icons:
Holy icons are a dogmatic confession in color, upheld by the Seventh Ecumenical Council. Because the Word became flesh, he can be depicted. We do not worship wood and pigment; we honor the prototype. The icon is a window and a presence, not an idol and not a mere illustration.

Iconoclasm is a Christological error. Parish walls teach the Bible and the saints to those who cannot read. Veneration of the icon passes to the one shown.
ortho.veneration:
Veneration, proskynesis, is honor given to the Cross, the Gospel, the icons, the relics, and the saints. Worship, latreia, is God's alone. The distinction is old and carefully kept, even when a hurried observer cannot see it.

We kiss the icon, bow, and light a candle. We do not confuse the saint with the Holy Trinity. Refusal of all veneration in the name of purity usually ends by refusing the Incarnation its consequences.
ortho.fasting:
Fasting is the Church's ascetic rule: Great Lent, the Apostles' Fast, Dormition, Nativity, and most Wednesdays and Fridays, with local shape. We abstain from certain foods to train the body, give to the poor, and make room for prayer. Fasting without mercy is rejected by the prophets and the Fathers.

The rule is a standard, applied with economy for the sick, the traveler, and the young. Fasting is joy, not display. It prepares for the Eucharist and for Pascha.
ortho.sacred_music:
Chant is the Church's sung word: Byzantine, Slavic, Georgian, Romanian, and other Orthodox traditions. The human voice carries the prayer. Harmony and folk beauty vary by land; the aim is the text of the feast, not a concert.

The choir or the chanter serves the altar. Performance that draws eyes to itself has missed the point. Silence is also music in the Liturgy.
ortho.instrumental_music:
Unaccompanied chant is the received Orthodox practice in the Liturgy. Organs and bands are not part of the classical rite. The voice of the Church is enough.

Some diaspora parishes have experimented; such experiments are not the mind of the rite. Instruments in a festival outside the altar are another question. At the Eucharist, the people sing.
ortho.preaching:
The homily opens the Scriptures and the feast to the people. It sits inside the Liturgy, usually after the Gospel. It is not a lecture that replaces the Anaphora, and not optional decoration.

Good preaching is doctrinal, moral, and pastoral, drawn from the Fathers as well as from the preacher's own wounds. Eloquence without obedience is a clanging cymbal. The bishop is the chief preacher of his church.
ortho.sign_of_the_cross:
The sign of the cross is the Orthodox Christian's constant confession: right to left in the received Eastern manner, with the fingers formed to speak the Trinity and the two natures. We sign ourselves at the Name, at the Gospel, in temptation, and at the table.

It is a small Creed in motion. Done in haste it can become a twitch; done with the mind it drives off the enemy and recalls Baptism. We also sign one another in blessing.
ortho.rosary:
The prayer rope, komboskini or chotki, is the monk's and the layperson's companion for the Jesus Prayer. Knots of wool are counted in secret. It is not a Latin rosary of mysteries, though some Orthodox use prayer beads in a kindred way.

The rope exists for attention, not for superstition. When the mind wanders, the knot brings it back to the Name.
ortho.jesus_prayer:
The Jesus Prayer is the prayer of the heart: 'Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, a sinner.' It is the shortest Gospel. Said with the breath, under a father's guidance, it can descend from the lips to the mind and to the heart.

It is not a technique for acquiring visions. It is repentance in a single sentence. Parishioners may use it; hesychast depths belong with obedience, not with curiosity.
ortho.mary:
The Theotokos, Panagia, Mother of God, is the first of the saints and the highest of creatures. She is not a fourth person of the Trinity. Every title given her is a title about Christ. If she is not Theotokos, her Son is not God in the flesh.

Orthodox love for her is liturgical and filial: hymns, icons, feasts, and the cry 'Most holy Theotokos, save us,' meaning her intercession. She always points to her Son. To ignore her is to thin the Gospel of the Incarnation.
ortho.theotokos:
Theotokos is the dogmatic name defined at Ephesus: she who gave birth to God. The Person born of her is the Word. Christotokos alone is not enough, because it can hide a division of the one Christ.

We call her Mother of God without saying she originated the Godhead. The name protects the union. Orthodox piety never tires of it because the Church never tires of the Incarnation.
ortho.immaculate_conception:
Orthodox honor the all-holy, immaculate, most blessed Theotokos, and they do not receive the Latin dogma of the Immaculate Conception as defined in the West. She is conceived as we are, in the fallen race, yet she is filled with grace and without personal sin. The difference turns on ancestral sin and on whether a separate privilege is needed.

Some Orthodox writers have used language that sounds close to the Latin teaching; the Church as a whole keeps the older instinct. Her purity is the Spirit's fruit in a human life, crowned at the Annunciation.
ortho.assumption:
The Dormition is the falling asleep of the Theotokos and her translation. The Church keeps August 15 as her Pascha. Tradition holds that she died a true death and that her body was not left to corruption, being taken into the heavens.

We do not require a late forensic definition to keep the feast. Icons show the apostles at her bier and Christ receiving her soul as a child. She goes before us into the resurrection we await.
ortho.perpetual_virginity:
The Theotokos is ever-virgin: before birth, in birth, and after birth. The 'brothers of the Lord' are read as kinsmen or Joseph's children from an earlier marriage, not as sons of Mary. The Church's hymnography is unambiguous.

This is not disdain for marriage. It is the confession that her womb became the temple of God and remained so. The Fathers bind this to the uniqueness of the Incarnation.
ortho.intercession_of_saints:
The intercession of the saints is the family prayer of the Church. Those who sleep in Christ are alive, and they pray. We ask their prayers as we ask a friend, only now a friend who stands nearer the throne.

This is not a second savior. There is one Mediator, Christ. The saints are his members. To refuse their intercession is often to treat death as stronger than the Body.
ortho.relics:
Holy relics are the bodies and belongings of the saints, honored because the Spirit dwelt in them and will raise them. God works healings through them as he did through Elisha's bones. They are not magic charms.

Every altar contains relics. We kiss them with the same honor we give icons. Contempt for relics is usually contempt for the body's future glory.
ortho.prayers_for_the_dead:
Prayers for the departed are the Church's mercy. We commemorate names at the Proskomedia, keep Saturdays of the dead, and sing memorials. Love does not stop at the grave. We ask rest and forgiveness for those who have gone before.

This is not a system of tariffs. It is communion. The departed pray for us; we pray for them. What God does with those prayers is his, and we do not need a map of every chamber of the afterlife to keep the duty.
ortho.canonization_of_saints:
Glorification of saints is the Church's recognition that God has already glorified a man or woman. Relics, miracles, a holy death, and the conscience of the people precede the synod's act. The Church does not make saints; she names them.

Local veneration can precede wider listing. No central office in one city owns the calendar. The saints are the Church's proof that theosis is not a theory.
ortho.heaven:
Heaven is communion with the Holy Trinity, the Kingdom already tasted in the Eucharist and awaited in fullness. It is not boredom on a cloud. It is the uncreated light, the city of the saints, the joy of seeing God as we are able.

Paradise is spoken of as the place of the righteous even now. The last word is the resurrection and the new creation, when heaven and earth are not two sealed rooms.
ortho.hell:
Hell is the experience of God's love as fire for those who have made themselves its enemies. Hades names the realm of the dead; Gehenna the final state of the lost. The Church warns of outer darkness and the worm that does not die.

Some Fathers emphasize God's desire that all be saved; some dwell on the tragedy of a freedom that refuses. Orthodox dogma does not require a detailed architecture of hell. It requires that we not treat judgment as a myth.
ortho.purgatory:
Orthodox reject a Latin purgatory conceived as a third place of satisfactory punishment with tariffs. We do pray for the departed and believe in a particular judgment after death. Images of aerial toll houses appear in some lives of saints and in popular piety; they are not a dogma, and Orthodox teachers disagree about how literally to take them.

What is firm is this: the soul meets the truth of its life, the prayers of the Church help, and the Last Judgment remains ahead. Between death and resurrection there is no vacation from God.
ortho.intermediate_state:
After death comes the particular judgment. The soul knows a foretaste of blessedness or of woe, often named paradise or Hades, while it awaits the resurrection of the body. This is not the end of the story.

The Church's prayers accompany the soul. Speculation about every stage should stay humble. The Fathers use images. The constant teaching is that personal existence continues, and that the body will catch up at the last day.
ortho.resurrection_of_the_dead:
We look for the resurrection of the dead. The same body, sown in corruption, will be raised in glory, as Christ's was. There is no final salvation that leaves the bones behind.

This hope judges every contempt for the body and every spiritualism that treats death as liberation from matter. The departed will not remain ghosts. Pascha is the pattern.
ortho.last_judgment:
The Last Judgment is the coming of Christ in glory, when all the dead are raised and the hidden things of every heart are brought to light. The sheep and the goats of the Gospel are not a children's story. Mercy and truth meet there.

Icons of the Judgment stand at the west wall of many churches so that we leave worship under that horizon. The criterion is love of the least of the brethren, which is love of Christ.
ortho.second_coming:
The Second Coming, the Parousia, is the blessed hope. He will come again in glory to judge the living and the dead. Orthodox piety does not date the day. It watches.

Chiliasm that binds the Kingdom to a worldly timetable has been rejected. The Lord comes suddenly. The Church prays 'Come, Lord Jesus' at every Eucharist, because the Liturgy is already his appearing in mystery.
ortho.annihilation:
The ordinary Orthodox confession is eternal punishment as well as eternal life, in the words of the Gospel and the Creed's horizon. Annihilation of the wicked is not the received dogma. A few writers have hoped for a final restoration of all; that hope has never been made the Church's definition and is often resisted.

We are forbidden to declare anyone finally lost. We are also forbidden to empty the Judge's warnings. The mystery of a freedom that can refuse God is left standing.
ortho.new_creation:
The new creation is the renewal of heaven and earth, not the discarding of the world God made. The cosmos will be transfigured as the body will be. Icons, blessing of waters and fruit, and the care of creation already hint at this.

History does not dissolve into spirit. It is gathered up. The Lamb is the lamp of that city. Our labor in the Lord is not in vain.
ortho.marriage:
Marriage is a holy calling, a Mystery in which a man and a woman become one flesh under the crown of martyrdom and joy. It is the domestic church. Continence and parenthood both have honor inside it according to strength and blessing.

It is not a sacrament only when children come, and it is not a private romance blessed after the fact. The crowning is public, ecclesial, and ordered to the Kingdom.
ortho.divorce:
Divorce is a tragedy the Church sometimes recognizes under economia when the union is already dead by adultery, abandonment, or other grave ruin. A second marriage may be blessed with a rite that tastes of penitence. A third is rarer and more shadowed. Indissolubility remains the norm; mercy remains the practice for the wounded.

There is no casual Orthodox divorce. The bishop's judgment, not the couple's impatience, governs the blessing of another union.
ortho.contraception:
Contraception is not defined by an Orthodox dogma parallel to modern Latin teaching. Abortifacient methods are rejected. Many synods and pastors now allow non-abortifacient means within marriage for serious reasons, under a father confessor, without blessing a selfish closing of the home to children. Other voices remain far stricter.

The constant notes are these: marriage is open to life, abortion is not family planning, and the couple does not decide alone as if the body were a machine.
ortho.abortion:
Abortion is the taking of an unborn child's life and is condemned as a grave sin. The Church's canons treat it with great severity and also open a long road of repentance. The mother's life in true medical peril is the hard case entrusted to spiritual and medical discernment, not to slogans.

The unborn bear the image of God. Parish life is called to support mothers so that the commandment is not only a prohibition.
ortho.sexual_ethics:
Chastity is wholeness: fidelity in marriage, abstinence outside it, and the refusal to treat the body as a tool of appetite. Fornication, adultery, and sexual use of persons as objects are sins to be confessed. Marriage is the place of the one-flesh union of man and woman.

The Church's teaching here is old and not a late reaction. Compassion for the struggler is commanded; rewriting the Mystery of Marriage is not. Fasting includes the eyes and the heart.
ortho.church_and_state:
Symphony is the classic Byzantine word: Church and empire, or Church and civil power, in concert without either swallowing the other. The Church crowns no ideology. She prays for civil authorities and reserves the right to disobey when they command sin.

History shows both fruitful cooperation and captivity. Autocephaly and nation often grew together; nationalism that makes the Church a department of the state is a heresy named phyletism. The Kingdom is not of this world, yet it is in this world.
ortho.ordination_of_women:
The Orthodox Church does not ordain women as bishops, priests, or deacons in the three-fold Holy Orders as now practiced worldwide. This is received as fidelity to the Lord's choosing and to unbroken practice, not as a statement that women lack the image of God or the gifts of the Spirit.

Women are saints, evangelists, abbesses, theologians, and the backbone of parish life. Debate about a restored female diaconate exists; it has not become a new settlement. The Theotokos is higher than the cherubim without being a priest at the altar.
ortho.headship:
Headship in household and church is read through Paul's image: the husband is head as Christ is head of the Church, which means the Cross, not domination. Mutual honor is the rule. Abuse is sin. The priest heads the parish under the bishop; he is not a petty tyrant.

Cultures have painted this teaching in their own colors, sometimes badly. The icon is Christ washing feet. Equality of nature and distinction of service can both be true.
ortho.head_covering:
Head covering for women in church is customary in many Orthodox lands and parishes, and rare in others. Where it is kept, it is a sign of reverence and of the angelic order of worship, not a proof of lesser dignity. Men uncover; women often cover.

Bishops set parish practice. The Apostle's words are still read. Uniform worldwide enforcement does not exist. The heart of the custom is modesty and the sense that we stand on holy ground.
ortho.roman_catholic_label:
Orthodox commonly say Roman Catholic or the Latins when naming the church in communion with the Pope of Rome. We do not concede that 'Catholic' without qualifier belongs only there, because we confess the Orthodox Church as catholic.

The term is descriptive of a real communion with its own theology and rites. It is not a slur in careful speech. Older polemical names exist; they are not required.
ortho.separated_brethren:
Those not in Orthodox communion are often called heterodox or non-Orthodox. The words mean 'of another opinion' or 'outside this communion,' not 'subhuman.' Some writers say 'other Christians'; some reserve 'Christian' more strictly. Practice in speech is not uniform.

We are commanded to speak the truth in love. Courtesy that pretends there is no schism is not love, and contempt is not Orthodoxy.
ortho.true_church_claim:
The Orthodox Church confesses herself to be the one holy catholic and apostolic Church. That claim is identical with her existence. It is not a branding exercise and not a denial that God works wherever he wills.

The proper use of the claim is repentance inside the house, not scorn outside it. If we are the Church, we must look like the Gospel. The invitation is to come and see, not to win an argument about labels.
